summary: Rakesh Bansal ordered 50 bags of Aashirvaad atta and 20 cartons of Maggi. He complained that last week's atta arrived three days late, which cost him two retailers to Patanjali. He also warned that Britannia gives 15-day credit against our 7 days, and that his order will halve next month unless we do something on credit. Arjun committed to delivery by Wednesday morning but did not address the credit issue.
score_reason: An order was taken and delivery was committed, but the credit threat went unaddressed, and there was no scheme talk, stock or visibility check, or collection at a strained account.

coaching.tip: You read back the order (20 cartons Maggi, 50 bags atta) and later gave a firm delivery time. That clarity helps rebuild trust after a late delivery.

When Rakesh ji raised Britannia's 15-day credit, you only said 'वो तो है'. Next time, ask how much volume is at stake, promise to take it to your manager, and give him a date for an answer, without promising any credit yourself.
For a wholesaler this size, also cover current schemes, check pending dues, ask which Patanjali SKUs retailers are switching to, and try to add Tata Tea or Parle-G to the order.

debrief: Arjun, Bansal Wholesale ka visit thoda tense tha. Rakesh ji late delivery aur credit se naraz the. Achhi baat: tumne pachaas bag atta aur bees carton Maggi ka order turant confirm karke repeat kiya. Agli baar jab Britannia ka pandrah din credit wala point aaye, sirf haan mat bolo. Manager se baat karke Rakesh ji ko ek date do. Next step: Wednesday subah tak delivery pakki karo, warehouse se baat karo, aur credit wali baat manager ko aaj hi batao.
